competitive_landscape: The Western Cyclades run today on conventional ferries (SeaJets, Blue Star and smaller local operators) — proof of real and fast-growing demand. The pain is sparse intra-loop sailings, meltemi cancellation of the exposed legs, and a diesel ride that punishes a high-spend, style-led guest. A quiet, on-demand foiling layer answers all three; no foiling operator runs here.

regulatory_note: Greek flag / EU; Hellenic Coast Guard certification and Greek cabotage rules favour EU-flagged vessels. Berths at Adamas (Milos) and the western port funds. EU maritime-decarbonisation policy adds a clean-fleet tailwind, and the design-hotel positioning aligns with low-emission, low-wake operation.
seasonality: Sharply seasonal (peak Jun–Sep) and meltemi-exposed — the open-water spoke east to Paros/Santorini is the most wind-sensitive leg, which is exactly where foiling flight above the chop delivers a smoother, more reliable ride than the fast ferry. The tight intra-western loop is more sheltered and workable across a longer season.

summary: Milos anchors the Western Cyclades, the design-hotel circuit widely billed as 'the next Santorini' — Milos, Kimolos, Sifnos and Serifos strung together by short hops that sit inside all-electric range. Arrivals are surging seasonally and the loop is tight and intra-cluster, while the high-value spoke east to the built Santorini and Paros nodes runs across exposed open water. A foiling layer turns the loop into one smooth, near-silent circuit and gives the design-hotel guest a reliable premium link to the rest of the Cyclades where the meltemi makes the fast ferry brutal.
tagline: The 'next Santorini' stylish-hotel circuit — a tight western Cyclades loop and a clean high-value spoke to the built marquee islands.
